questionText: Siya buys 11 stickers at Rs.25 each. What is the total cost?
hints: Every sticker costs the same, so this is a multiplication problem. The total cost is the price of one item times the number of items.
Multiply 25 by 11. A handy way is to find 10 lots of 25 first and then add 1 more lot.
Here is a similar one: 12 pencils at Rs.20 each. 10 × 20 = 200 and 2 × 20 = 40, so the total is 200 + 40 = 240, which is Rs.240.

stepByStep.text: Each sticker costs Rs.25 and Siya buys 11 of them, so multiply 25 by 11.
Add the two parts: 250 + 25 = 275.
The total cost is Rs.275.

misconceptions.A: 264 is 11 × 24, so the price has slipped by 1. Each sticker costs Rs.25, so work out 11 × 25.
misconceptions.B: 36 is 11 + 25. Siya pays Rs.25 eleven times over, so the two numbers must be multiplied, not added.
misconceptions.C: Great job! 11 stickers at Rs.25 each cost 11 × 25 = 275 rupees.
misconceptions.D: 300 is 12 × 25, which is the cost of 12 stickers. Siya buys 11, so the total is one sticker less.

stepByStep.text: Each eraser costs Rs.15 and Siddharth buys 12 of them, so multiply 15 by 12.
Add the two parts: 150 + 30 = 180.

misconceptions.A: 168 is 12 × 14, so the price has slipped by 1. Each eraser costs Rs.15, so work out 12 × 15.
misconceptions.B: You got it! 12 erasers at Rs.15 each cost 12 × 15 = 180 rupees.
misconceptions.C: 27 is 12 + 15. Siddharth pays Rs.15 twelve times over, so the two numbers must be multiplied, not added.
misconceptions.D: 195 is 13 × 15, which is the cost of 13 erasers. Siddharth buys 12, so the total is one eraser less.

questionText: Isha buys 10 pens at Rs.10 each. What is the total cost?
hints: Every pen costs the same, so this is a multiplication problem. The total cost is the price of one item times the number of items.
Multiply the price of one pen by the number of pens. Multiplying a number by 10 moves each digit one place to the left and puts a 0 in the ones place.

stepByStep.text: Each pen costs Rs.10 and Isha buys 10 of them, so multiply 10 by 10.
Ten tens make one hundred.
The total cost is Rs.100.

misconceptions.B: 90 is 9 × 10, which is the cost of 9 pens. Isha buys 10 pens.

misconceptions.D: Well done! 10 pens at Rs.10 each cost 10 × 10 = 100 rupees.

questionText: Neha buys a book for Rs.60 and sells it at a profit of 10%. What is the selling price?
hints: A profit makes the selling price more than the cost price, and a loss makes it less. First you need the profit in rupees.
Find 10% of 60 rupees. 10% means 10 out of every 100.
Here is a similar one. A lamp is bought for 200 rupees and sold at a profit of 30%. 30% of 200 is 200 × 30 ÷ 100 = 60 rupees. The selling price is 200 + 60 = 260 rupees.

stepByStep.text: 10% means 10 out of every 100. So 10% of 60 is 60 × 10 ÷ 100 = 6 rupees.
That is the profit, so add it to the cost price: 60 + 6 = 66. The selling price is 66 rupees.

misconceptions.A: 6 is only the profit, 10% of 60. The selling price is the cost and the profit together.
misconceptions.B: 60 is the cost price. With a profit, the selling price must be more than 60.
misconceptions.C: 70 is 60 + 10, but 10% is not 10 rupees. Find what 10% of 60 comes to first.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 10% of 60 is 6 rupees of profit, and 60 + 6 = 66.

hints: This sum mixes division, addition and multiplication. The order matters: division and multiplication are done before addition.

questionText: Rohan buys 8 books at Rs.3 each. What is the total cost?
hints: Every book costs the same, so this is a multiplication problem. The total cost is the price of one item times the number of items.
Multiply the price of one book by the number of books. This is a fact from the 3 times table.
Here is a similar one: 6 toys at Rs.7 each cost 6 × 7 = 42, which is Rs.42.

stepByStep.text: Each book costs Rs.3 and Rohan buys 8 of them, so multiply 3 by 8.
Eight threes are twenty-four.
The total cost is Rs.24.

misconceptions.A: 27 is 9 × 3, which is the cost of 9 books. Rohan buys 8 books.

questionText: Riya bought a bicycle for Rs.500 and sold it at a loss of 25%. What is the selling price?
hints: A profit makes the selling price more than the cost price, and a loss makes it less. First you need the loss in rupees.
Find 25% of 500 rupees. 25% means 25 out of every 100.
Here is a similar one. A bag is bought for 300 rupees and sold at a loss of 20%. 20% of 300 is 300 × 20 ÷ 100 = 60 rupees. The selling price is 300 − 60 = 240 rupees.

stepByStep.text: 25% means 25 out of every 100. So 25% of 500 is 500 × 25 ÷ 100 = 125 rupees.
That is the loss, so take it away from the cost price: 500 − 125 = 375. The selling price is 375 rupees.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 25% of 500 is 125 rupees lost, and 500 − 125 = 375.
misconceptions.B: 625 is 500 + 125, which would be a profit. A loss means the selling price is less than the cost.
misconceptions.C: 500 is the cost price. With a loss, the selling price must be less than 500.
misconceptions.D: 125 is only the loss, 25% of 500. The selling price is what remains of the cost after the loss.

hints: This is an order of operations problem. Brackets come first, and inside a bracket multiplication comes before addition.

Here is a similar one: {(1 + 4) × 3} − (1 + 4 × 3). The first part is 5 × 3 = 15. The second part is 1 + 12 = 13. Then 15 − 13 = 2.

questionText: Raunak buys 12 dozen, Shail buys 5 score. Who has more and by how much?
hints: Dozen and score are names for groups. Change both amounts into plain numbers so that you can compare them.
One dozen is 12 and one score is 20. Multiply to find how many each child has.

stepByStep.text: One dozen is 12, and Raunak has 12 dozen.
One score is 20, and Shail has 5 score.
Raunak has more. Subtract to find how many more.
Raunak has more, by 44.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Raunak has 144 and Shail has 100, so Raunak has 44 more.
misconceptions.B: A score is 20, so Shail has 5 × 20 = 100. Raunak has 12 × 12 = 144, which is more.
misconceptions.C: Raunak does have more, but check the amounts. 12 dozen is 144 and 5 score is 100.
misconceptions.D: They are not equal. 12 dozen is 144 and 5 score is 100.

misconceptions.D: This would be a whole empty box. The last box already holds 20 oranges.

questionText: Which of these products is the greatest?
hints: Before multiplying, look at what the four pairs have in common. Try the same idea with much smaller numbers to see a pattern.
Add the two numbers in each pair. Then try small pairs with the same total, such as 5 × 5, 4 × 6 and 3 × 7, and see which is biggest.

A similar problem: which is greatest, 10 × 10, 9 × 11 or 8 × 12? Each pair adds up to 20. The products are 100, 99 and 96. The closer together the two numbers are, the bigger the product, so 10 × 10 is greatest.

stepByStep.text: Each pair of numbers adds up to 100.
When two numbers have the same total, their product is biggest when the numbers are closest together. Small numbers show this: 5 × 5 = 25, 4 × 6 = 24, 3 × 7 = 21.
Check with the nearest pair.
The greatest product is 50 × 50.

misconceptions.A: Well done! All the pairs add up to 100, and the equal pair gives the biggest product, 2500.
misconceptions.B: This pair has the largest single number, 53, but its partner 47 is small. The product is 2491, the smallest of the four.
misconceptions.C: This is very close: 49 × 51 = 2499, just 1 less than the greatest.
misconceptions.D: 48 × 52 = 2496. A pair whose numbers are closer together gives a little more.

questionText: Which sign must go in the box to make this true?  6 + 12 □ 3 × 2 = 12  (The usual order of operations is followed.)
hints: Test each sign in the box. Each time, do the multiplying and dividing first, then the adding and subtracting from left to right.
Whatever sign goes in the box, 3 × 2 or 12 ÷ 3 × 2 is worked out before anything is added to 6. Start by trying ÷ with care.
A similar problem: 4 + 10 □ 2 × 3 = 8. Try −: the multiplication comes first, 2 × 3 = 6, then 4 + 10 − 6 = 8. So the sign is −. With ÷ it would be 10 ÷ 2 × 3 = 15, and 4 + 15 = 19.

stepByStep.text: Try ÷. The dividing and multiplying are done first.
Try −. The multiplication is done first.
The other two signs give 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 and 6 + 72 = 78.
The sign in the box must be − (subtract).

misconceptions.A: Working from left to right gives 18 ÷ 3 × 2 = 12, but the division and multiplication come before the addition: 6 + 8 = 14.
misconceptions.B: With × the value is 6 + 12 × 3 × 2 = 6 + 72 = 78, which is far too big.
misconceptions.C: With + the value is 6 + 12 + 6 = 24. The result must be 12.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! 3 × 2 = 6 is done first, and 6 + 12 − 6 = 12.

questionText: In which of these can the brackets be removed without changing the value?
hints: Brackets tell you what to do first. They are not needed when the part inside them would be done first anyway.
For each choice, ask: without the brackets, which operation comes first by the order of operations? Is it the same one that is inside the brackets?

A similar problem: in 20 − (3 × 5) the multiplication would be done first even without brackets, so 20 − 3 × 5 = 5 both ways. In 20 − (3 + 5) the value is 12, but 20 − 3 + 5 is 22, so those brackets are needed.

stepByStep.text: In 12 − (4 × 2), the multiplication is done first with or without brackets.
In 12 − (4 + 2) the value changes from 6 to 10 when the brackets go.
In (12 − 4) × 2 the value changes from 16 to 4, and in 12 ÷ (4 + 2) it changes from 2 to 5.
The brackets can be removed only in 12 − (4 × 2).

misconceptions.A: Well done! Multiplication comes before subtraction anyway, so the value is 4 with or without the brackets.
misconceptions.B: With the brackets this is 12 − 6 = 6. Without them it is 12 − 4 + 2 = 10, because we work from left to right.
misconceptions.C: With the brackets this is 8 × 2 = 16. Without them the multiplication comes first: 12 − 8 = 4.
misconceptions.D: With the brackets this is 12 ÷ 6 = 2. Without them the division comes first: 3 + 2 = 5.

questionText: Pencils cost ₹4 each and pens cost ₹9 each. Rohit buys 10 of these in all and pays exactly ₹60. How many pens does he buy?
hints: Imagine that everything he bought was the cheaper thing. Then see how much the bill goes up each time one of them is swapped for the dearer thing.
If all 10 were pencils, the bill would be 10 × ₹4. Find how much more than this Rohit paid.

A similar problem: balls cost ₹3 and bats cost ₹8, and 6 things cost ₹33. If all were balls the bill would be 6 × 3 = ₹18. The extra is 33 − 18 = ₹15. Each bat adds 8 − 3 = ₹5, so there are 15 ÷ 5 = 3 bats.

stepByStep.text: If all 10 were pencils, the bill would be ₹40.
Rohit paid ₹20 more than that.
Each pen costs ₹5 more than a pencil, so find how many pens make up the extra.
Check: 4 pens and 6 pencils cost 36 + 24 = 60. He buys 4 pens.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 4 pens cost ₹36 and 6 pencils cost ₹24, which makes ₹60.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of pencils. The question asks how many pens he buys.
misconceptions.C: 5 pens and 5 pencils would cost 45 + 20 = ₹65, which is too much.
misconceptions.D: 2 pens and 8 pencils would cost 18 + 32 = ₹50, which is too little.

questionText: Kiran had to divide a number by 6. By mistake she multiplied it by 6 and got 432. What answer should she have got?
hints: First find the number Kiran started with by undoing what she did. Then do what she was supposed to do.
Kiran multiplied by 6 and got 432. Undo this by dividing 432 by 6 to find her number.
A similar problem: Mohan had to divide a number by 4 but multiplied by 4 and got 80. His number was 80 ÷ 4 = 20, so he should have got 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

stepByStep.text: Undo the multiplication to find the number Kiran started with.
Now do what she was supposed to do: divide the number by 6.
Kiran should have got 12.

misconceptions.A: This is the number Kiran started with. She still has to divide it by 6.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! The number was 72, and 72 ÷ 6 = 12.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 432 by 6 again. To undo a multiplication by 6, divide by 6.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 6 from 432. Undo the multiplication by dividing, then divide once more.

questionText: Insert the proper sign of comparison in the box: 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8+9 □ 5×7
hints: To choose the sign, you need the value of each side. Work out the left side and the right side separately, and then compare the two numbers.
Add the numbers from 1 to 9. A quick way is to pair them so that each pair makes 10, such as 1 and 9, or 2 and 8. Then work out 5 × 7.
Here is a similar one: compare 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 with 4 × 6. The left side is 21 and the right side is 24. Since 21 is less than 24, the sign would be <.

stepByStep.text: On the left side, pair the numbers to make tens: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6. That is four tens, which is 40, and the 5 in the middle makes 45.
On the right side, multiply.
45 is greater than 35, so the sign in the box is >.

misconceptions.A: For this sign the two sides would need to have the same value. The left side adds up to 45 and the right side is 35, so they are not equal.
misconceptions.B: Great job! The left side is 45 and the right side is 35, and 45 is greater than 35.
misconceptions.C: This sign says the left side is smaller. The left side is 45 and the right side is 35, so the left side is the bigger one.
misconceptions.D: One of the three signs always fits a pair of numbers. Work out both sides, which are 45 and 35, and compare them.

questionText: A bottle contains 150 ml of cough syrup. The doctor prescribes 25ml each day. How many days will the cough syrup last for?
hints: The syrup is used up in equal amounts each day. Finding how many equal parts fit into a total is a division problem.
Divide the amount in the bottle, 150 ml, by the amount taken each day, 25 ml. You can also count up in 25s until you reach 150.
Here is a similar one: a bottle holds 120 ml and 30 ml is taken each day. 120 ÷ 30 = 4, so that bottle lasts for 4 days.

stepByStep.text: The bottle holds 150 ml and 25 ml is taken each day, so divide 150 by 25.
Count up in 25s: 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150. That is 6 lots of 25.
The cough syrup will last for 6 days.

misconceptions.A: 8 days would need 8 × 25 = 200 ml, which is more than the bottle holds. Count how many 25s make 150.
misconceptions.B: You got it! 6 lots of 25 ml make 150 ml, so the syrup lasts for 6 days.
misconceptions.C: 3 days would use only 3 × 25 = 75 ml, which is half the bottle. Keep counting in 25s up to 150.
misconceptions.D: 5 days would use 5 × 25 = 125 ml, so 25 ml would still be left. That is enough for one more day.

questionText: A fruit seller purchases three baskets of oranges marked A, B and C on the baskets. A contains 16 more oranges than C and B contains 12 more than the sum of A and C. If C contains 22 oranges, how many oranges did the fruit seller purchase?
hints: This is a word problem with several steps. One basket is known, and the other two are described by comparing them with it, so work out the baskets one at a time.
Start with basket C, which has 22 oranges, and use it to find basket A. Basket B depends on A and C together, so leave it until last.

Here is a similar one with three boxes of pencils, P, Q and R. R has 10. P has 5 more than R, so P has 15. Q has 4 more than the sum of P and R, so Q has 15 + 10 + 4 = 29. Altogether there are 15 + 29 + 10 = 54 pencils.

stepByStep.text: Basket C has 22 oranges. Basket A has 16 more than C.
Find the sum of A and C.
Basket B has 12 more than that sum.
Add all three baskets.
The trap is that B is compared with A and C together, not with just one of them. The fruit seller purchased 132 oranges.

misconceptions.A: Excellent thinking! The baskets hold 38, 72 and 22 oranges, and 38 + 72 + 22 = 132.
misconceptions.B: 112 is too few. Check basket B: it holds 12 more than A and C put together, which is 60 + 12.
misconceptions.C: 100 is too few. Basket A holds 22 + 16 oranges, and basket B holds 12 more than A and C put together.
misconceptions.D: The total is one of the numbers given. Find A as 22 + 16, then B as 12 more than A and C together, and add all three baskets.

questionText: A shopkeeper buys 6 gross of pencils. He packs them in boxes which can contain a dozen of these pencils. How many boxes will be packed?
hints: This problem uses two counting words. A dozen is 12 things, and a gross is 12 dozen.
Since one gross is 12 dozen, work out how many dozens there are in 6 gross. Each box holds exactly one dozen.
Here is a similar one: 4 gross of erasers are packed in boxes of a dozen. One gross is 12 dozen, so 4 gross is 4 × 12 = 48 dozen, and 48 boxes are needed.

stepByStep.text: One gross is 12 dozen, and a dozen is 12. So one gross is 12 × 12 = 144 pencils.
6 gross is 6 lots of 144 pencils.
Each box holds a dozen, which is 12 pencils, so divide by 12.
A quicker way is to see that 6 gross is 6 × 12 = 72 dozen, and each dozen fills one box. So 72 boxes will be packed.

misconceptions.A: 80 is too many. One gross is 12 dozen, so 6 gross is 6 × 12 dozen, and each dozen fills one box.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 6 gross is 6 × 12 = 72 dozen, and each dozen fills one box.
misconceptions.C: 64 is too few. One gross is 12 dozen, so count 12 boxes for every gross.
misconceptions.D: 36 is 6 × 6. A gross is 12 dozen, not 6 dozen, so each gross fills 12 boxes.

questionText: Which of the following can be the product of (★★7) and (★★8) where ★ denotes digits not necessarily the same?
hints: You cannot know the two numbers, but you can still tell things about their product. Think about what its last digit must be, and about how big or how small it can be.
The numbers end in 7 and 8, so find the last digit of 7 × 8. Then think about how many digits the product of two three-digit numbers can have.

Here is a similar one with two-digit numbers (★3) and (★4). Since 3 × 4 = 12, the product ends in 2. Two two-digit numbers multiply to at least 10 × 10 = 100 and to less than 100 × 100 = 10000, so the product has three or four digits. A number like 552 fits, and in fact 23 × 24 = 552.

stepByStep.text: The last digit of a product comes from the last digits of the two numbers. 7 × 8 = 56, so the product must end in 6. That rules out 10552, which ends in 2.
Both numbers have three digits, so each is at least 100. Their product is at least 100 × 100 = 10000, which has five digits. That rules out 9786, which has only four digits.
Each number is less than 1000, so the product is less than 1000 × 1000 = 1000000. That rules out 9950006, which has seven digits.
The only number left ends in 6 and is the right size. In fact it can be made.
Checking the last digit and the number of digits shows that the product can be 308256.

misconceptions.A: 10552 ends in 2. The two numbers end in 7 and 8, and 7 × 8 = 56, so their product must end in 6.
misconceptions.B: 9786 does end in 6, but it has only four digits. Two three-digit numbers multiply to at least 100 × 100 = 10000.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! It ends in 6 and is the right size, and in fact 507 × 608 = 308256.
misconceptions.D: 9950006 does end in 6, but it has seven digits. Two three-digit numbers multiply to less than 1000 × 1000 = 1000000.

hints: This sum mixes four operations. Multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction.
Find the multiplication and the division in the sum and work those two out first. Then go from left to right with what is left.
Here is a similar one: 8 + 3 × 6 − 10 ÷ 5. First 3 × 6 = 18 and 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Then 8 + 18 = 26, and 26 − 2 = 24.

stepByStep.text: Do the multiplication first.
Do the division next.
The sum is now 6 + 20 − 3. Go from left to right: 6 + 20 = 26, and then 26 − 3 = 23.

misconceptions.A: 10 comes from working out 6 + 20 − 6 and then dividing everything by 2. Only the 6 just before the division sign is divided by 2.
misconceptions.B: 19 comes from working strictly from left to right: 11, then 44, then 38, then 19. Multiplication and division must be done before addition and subtraction.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 5 × 4 is 20 and 6 ÷ 2 is 3, and 6 + 20 − 3 = 23.
misconceptions.D: 13 is half of 26, so it looks as if all of 6 + 5 × 4 was divided by 2. Only the 6 just before the division sign is divided, and that 3 is then taken away from 26.

questionText: Where should the bracket be put to make the following equation true: 5 × 7 + 3 − 10 = 40
hints: Brackets change the order of a sum, because whatever is inside a bracket is done first. The task is to find the bracket that makes the left side come to 40.
Try each way of placing the bracket in turn. Work out the bracket first, and then follow the usual order: multiplication before addition and subtraction. See which one gives 40.

Here is a similar one: where should the bracket go to make 4 × 6 + 2 − 5 = 27 true? Without a bracket the left side is 24 + 2 − 5 = 21. With a bracket around 6 + 2 it becomes 4 × 8 − 5, and 32 − 5 = 27. So the bracket goes around 6 + 2.

stepByStep.text: Without any bracket, 5 × 7 = 35 is done first, and 35 + 3 − 10 = 28. That is not 40.
A bracket around 5 × 7, or around 5 × 7 + 3, does not change the order, so the result is still 28.
A bracket around 7 + 3 − 10 comes to 0, and 5 × 0 = 0.
A bracket around 7 + 3 comes to 10. Then 5 × 10 = 50, and 50 − 10 = 40.
The bracket has to make the addition happen before the multiplication. So the bracket goes around (7 + 3).

misconceptions.A: A bracket around 5 × 7 changes nothing, because the multiplication is done first anyway. The sum still comes to 35 + 3 − 10 = 28.
misconceptions.B: This bracket comes to 0, and 5 × 0 is 0. Try a bracket that makes the 5 multiply a bigger number.
misconceptions.C: Inside this bracket 5 × 7 is still done first, which gives 38, and 38 − 10 = 28. The bracket needs to make the addition happen before the multiplication.
misconceptions.D: Great job! The bracket makes 7 + 3 into 10, and then 5 × 10 = 50 and 50 − 10 = 40.

hints: This sum has a bracket and four operations. The bracket is done first, and inside it the usual order still applies: multiply and divide before you add or subtract.
Start inside the bracket with 2 × 4 and 15 ÷ 3, and then subtract. After that, look outside the bracket and do the multiplication before going from left to right.
Here is a similar one: 20 − 4 × 3 + (2 × 5 − 8 ÷ 4). Inside the bracket, 2 × 5 = 10 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so the bracket is 10 − 2 = 8. Outside, 4 × 3 = 12. Then 20 − 12 = 8, and 8 + 8 = 16.

stepByStep.text: Start inside the bracket, with the multiplication and the division: 2 × 4 = 8 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5.
Finish the bracket.
Outside the bracket, multiply.
The sum is now 9 − 6 + 3. Go from left to right: 9 − 6 = 3, and then 3 + 3 = 6.
The trap is to do 9 − 3 first, or to take the bracket away instead of adding it. The answer is 6.

misconceptions.A: 10 is too big. The bracket comes to 8 − 5 = 3, and outside it 3 × 2 is 6, so the sum becomes 9 − 6 + 3.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! The bracket is 3 and 3 × 2 is 6, and 9 − 6 + 3 = 6.
misconceptions.C: 15 comes from doing 9 − 3 first and then multiplying by 2. Multiplication comes before subtraction, so find 3 × 2 first.
misconceptions.D: 0 comes from taking the bracket away, as in 9 − 6 − 3. The sign in front of the bracket is a plus, so its 3 is added.

hints: Every part of this sum is a number multiplied by 7. When the same number is multiplied each time, you can collect the other numbers first and multiply by 7 just once.
Either work out each of the four products and then add and subtract from left to right, or count how many 7s there are altogether: 11 sevens and 13 sevens, take away 6 sevens, and 2 sevens more.
Here is a similar one: 9 × 5 + 6 × 5 − 5 × 4 + 1 × 5. Count the fives: 9 + 6 − 4 + 1 = 12. Then 12 × 5 = 60.

stepByStep.text: Work out each product: 11 × 7 = 77, 13 × 7 = 91, 7 × 6 = 42 and 2 × 7 = 14.
Now go from left to right: 77 + 91 = 168, then 168 − 42 = 126, then 126 + 14 = 140.
As a quick check, there are 11 + 13 − 6 + 2 = 20 sevens altogether.
Both ways give the same result, so the answer is 140.

misconceptions.A: 144 is close. Check each product again: they are 77, 91, 42 and 14, and the 42 is the one that is taken away.
misconceptions.B: Well done! There are 20 sevens altogether, and 20 × 7 = 140.
misconceptions.C: 198 is too big. The 7 × 6 part has a minus sign in front of it, so 42 is taken away from the total.
misconceptions.D: 224 comes from adding all four products. The 7 × 6 part has a minus sign in front of it, so 42 must be taken away, not added.

questionText: According to the BODMAS Rule, which of the following is correct?
hints: Each choice is a little sum with a result. To test one, work out its left side yourself in the BODMAS order and see whether you get the number shown.
Take the statements one at a time. Do brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Compare your result with the number after the equals sign.
Here is a similar one: is it true that 3 + 4 × 5 comes to 35? Multiply first: 4 × 5 = 20, and then 3 + 20 = 23. So that statement is not true; 35 comes from adding first.

stepByStep.text: In 2 × 7 − 5, multiply first: 2 × 7 is 14, and 14 − 5 = 9. The statement says 4, so it is not true.
In 5 + 5 × 25, multiply first: 5 × 25 is 125, and 5 + 125 = 130. The statement says 250, so it is not true.
In (18 + 7) ÷ 7, the bracket is 25, and 25 ÷ 7 is 3 with 4 left over. The statement says 19, so it is not true.
Not one of the three statements is true, so the answer is None of these.

misconceptions.A: This statement gives 4, which comes from doing 7 − 5 first. Multiply first: 2 × 7 is 14, and 14 − 5 is 9.
misconceptions.B: This statement gives 250, which comes from adding 5 + 5 first. Multiply first: 5 × 25 is 125, and 5 + 125 is 130.
misconceptions.C: This statement gives 19, which comes from dividing 7 by 7 before using the bracket. The bracket comes first: 18 + 7 is 25, and 25 ÷ 7 is not 19.
misconceptions.D: Well checked! The three sums really come to 9, 130 and 25 ÷ 7, so not one of the statements is true.

questionText: Which of the following can be the product of (★ ★ 8) and (★ ★ 7) where ★ denote digits not necessarily the same?
hints: You do not need to find the hidden digits. Think about what the last digit of the product must be, and about how small or how big the product of two three-digit numbers can be.
Multiply just the two last digits, 8 and 7, to see which digit the product must end in. Set aside any choice that ends in a different digit, and then test the sizes of the ones that are left.

Here is a similar one with two-digit numbers: which of 96, 152 and 312 can be (★ 3) × (★ 4)? Since 3 × 4 = 12, the product must end in 2, so 96 is out. The smallest such product is 13 × 14 = 182, so 152 is too small. That leaves 312, and 13 × 24 = 312.

stepByStep.text: The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. Here 8 × 7 = 56, so the product must end in 6.
11558 ends in 8, so it cannot be the product. The other three numbers all end in 6, so now look at their sizes.
Both numbers have three digits, so the smallest they can be is 108 and 107. Their product is 11556, so 10556 is too small.
Both numbers are less than 1000, so their product is less than 1000 × 1000 = 1000000. The number 9995006 is bigger than that, so it is too big.
Only 36846 is left, and it really can be made: 178 × 207 = 36846. So the product can be 36846.

misconceptions.A: Look at the last digits. 8 × 7 = 56, so the product has to end in 6, but 11558 ends in 8.
misconceptions.B: The last digit 6 fits, so check the size. Even the smallest pair, 108 and 107, multiply to 11556, which is already more than 10556.
misconceptions.C: The last digit 6 fits, so check the size. Two numbers below 1000 always multiply to less than 1000000, and 9995006 is far more than that.
misconceptions.D: Yes! It ends in 6, just as 8 × 7 = 56 needs, it is the right size, and 178 × 207 = 36846.

hints: This sum has a bracket, a division, a multiplication and two additions. Remember the order: the bracket first, then dividing and multiplying, and adding last.
Start inside the bracket. Even in there, do 3 × 2 before you add it to 19.
Here is a similar one: (14 + 2 × 5) ÷ 6 + 3 × 2. Inside the bracket, 2 × 5 = 10 and 14 + 10 = 24. Then 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 3 × 2 = 6. Last, 4 + 6 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Start inside the bracket, and multiply before you add: 3 × 2 = 6, and then 19 + 6 = 25.
Now the sum reads 25 ÷ 5 + 4 × 3. The trap is to add the 4 too early. Divide and multiply first: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 and 4 × 3 = 12.
Add the two results last: 5 + 12 = 17. The answer is 17.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The bracket comes to 25, then 25 ÷ 5 = 5 and 4 × 3 = 12, and 5 + 12 = 17.
misconceptions.B: Check each part again. The bracket should come to 25, then work out 25 ÷ 5 and 4 × 3 separately and add those two answers.
misconceptions.C: It looks as if 5 was taken away from the bracket instead of dividing by it. The sign is ÷, so work out 25 ÷ 5, and then add 4 × 3.
misconceptions.D: This comes from adding 5 + 4 first and then multiplying by 3. Multiply 4 × 3 first, and then add the 5.

questionText: In a cinema hall each row has 17 seats and the rows are named from A to Q. If 3 seats are vacant in each of the rows from A to H. How many people seated in the cinema hall?
hints: First find how many seats there are in all. Then take away the empty ones.
Count the rows from A to Q. Multiply by 17 seats to get the total. Then count the rows from A to H to find how many seats are empty.

Here is a similar one. A hall has rows A to J, which is 10 rows, with 12 seats each. That is 10 × 12 = 120 seats. If 2 seats are empty in each of rows A to E, that is 5 × 2 = 10 empty seats. So 120 − 10 = 110 people are seated.

stepByStep.text: Rows A to Q make 17 rows, because Q is the 17th letter of the alphabet.
Find the total number of seats.
Rows A to H make 8 rows, each with 3 empty seats.
Take away the empty seats.
265 people are seated.

misconceptions.A: Check the count of rows. A to Q is 17 rows and A to H is 8 rows. Then subtract 24 from 289.
misconceptions.B: This is close. The empty seats are 8 × 3 = 24. Subtract 24 from 289.
misconceptions.C: Check the total first. 17 × 17 = 289. Then take away the 24 empty seats.
misconceptions.D: Yes! There are 17 × 17 = 289 seats and 8 × 3 = 24 are empty, so 289 − 24 = 265.

questionText: Insert the bracket in proper place so that the equality is true: 48 ÷ 8 − 2 + 5 = 13
hints: A bracket changes which part of a sum is done first. Try the bracket around each possible part and see which one makes the sum come to 13.
First work the sum out with no bracket at all, to see what it gives. Then ask which part, if it were done first, would make the total bigger.
Here is a similar one: put a bracket in 36 ÷ 6 − 2 + 1 so that it equals 10. With a bracket around 6 − 2, the sum becomes 36 ÷ 4 + 1. Then 36 ÷ 4 = 9 and 9 + 1 = 10, so the bracket goes around 6 − 2.

stepByStep.text: With no bracket, the division comes first: 48 ÷ 8 = 6, then 6 − 2 = 4 and 4 + 5 = 9. That is not 13, so the bracket must change the order.
A bracket around 48 ÷ 8 − 2, or around 48 ÷ 8, changes nothing, because those parts were already done first. The sum still comes to 9.
A bracket around 2 + 5 turns the sum into 48 ÷ 8 − 7. That is 6 take away 7, which is less than zero, so it cannot be 13.
A bracket around 8 − 2 turns the sum into 48 ÷ 6 + 5. Then 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 8 + 5 = 13, which is what we want.
So the bracket goes around 8 − 2, written (8 − 2).

misconceptions.A: This bracket holds the parts that are done first anyway, so nothing changes: 48 ÷ 8 = 6, 6 − 2 = 4 and 4 + 5 = 9. Look for a bracket that changes the number you divide by.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Doing 8 − 2 = 6 first gives 48 ÷ 6 = 8, and 8 + 5 = 13.
misconceptions.C: Division is already done first, so this bracket changes nothing and the sum still comes to 9. Try the bracket in a place where it changes the order.
misconceptions.D: With this bracket the sum is 48 ÷ 8 − 7, which is 6 take away 7. That is less than zero, not 13. Try making the number you divide by smaller instead.

hints: Every number here is 8, so the only thing to watch is the order of the four signs. Multiplying and dividing are done before adding and subtracting.
Find the multiplication and the division in the sum and work those two parts out first. Leave the adding and the subtracting until afterwards.
Here is a similar one: 6 + 6 × 6 − 6 ÷ 6. First 6 × 6 = 36 and 6 ÷ 6 = 1. Now the sum reads 6 + 36 − 1. Then 6 + 36 = 42 and 42 − 1 = 41.

stepByStep.text: Do the multiplication and the division first: 8 × 8 = 64 and 8 ÷ 8 = 1.
Now the sum reads 8 + 64 − 1. Go from left to right: 8 + 64 = 72.
Then take away the 1: 72 − 1 = 71. The answer is 71.

misconceptions.A: Check the order of the steps. Work out 8 × 8 and 8 ÷ 8 first, then add and subtract. The total is much more than 0.
misconceptions.B: This comes from going straight from left to right: 8 + 8 = 16, 16 × 8 = 128, 128 − 8 = 120 and 120 ÷ 8 = 15. Multiply and divide first instead.
misconceptions.C: You found 8 × 8 = 64 and took away the 1. The 8 at the front still has to be added.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 8 × 8 = 64 and 8 ÷ 8 = 1 come first, and then 8 + 64 − 1 = 71.

questionText: Which of the following can be the product of (★ ★ 7) and (★ ★ 6) where ★ denotes digits not necessarily the same?
hints: You do not need to find the hidden digits. Think about the last digit of the product and about how big the product can be.
Both numbers have three digits. Multiply only their last digits, 7 and 6, to see what the product must end in. Then think how many digits the product of two 3-digit numbers can have.
